name: Tales of the Rupee
description:
This talk traces the rupee’s five-hundred-year journey across India and beyond, from 1538 to its modern, digital forms. Drawing on a landmark exhibition and the accompanying publication, Odyssey of the Rupee: From India to the World, the session explores how a single denomination carries within it entire histories of economics, commerce, empire, and identity. What can a coin, passed from hand to hand across centuries, still tell us about where we come from? 
Bringing perspectives of numismatists, economists, and historians from the book, the talk examines coinage as more than just currency, but rather as evidence; a material record of the political and economic forces that have shaped our reality. Marking the Republic of India’s rupee at seventy-five years, the session situates this anniversary within a far longer arc, inviting the audience to see the coin in their pocket as the latest chapter in a story centuries in the making.

name: The Custodians of the Bengaluru Dose
description:
Language: English and Kannada 
Crisp on the outside, soft and spongy on the inside, and delicious all round, the Bengaluru dose has been a defining symbol of the city for over a century. This conversation brings together the custodians of two of Bengaluru’s generational eateries, the century-old Udupi Sri Krishna Bhavan and the eighty-three-year-old Vidyarthi Bhavan, to reveal the challenges of staying relevant in a global city with a whimsical and adventurous palate, and the joys of keeping a longstanding tradition alive. 
The dose did not earn its place by accident. It owes its dominance to the quiet, painstaking work of family-run restaurants, who have ensured over generations that the dose and its companions, chutney, palya, and sambar, never fall below the dizzyingly high standards set by their founders. In an increasingly crowded dosa-scape of Mysore masale, Davangere benne, and Mylari, of upstarts like ghee podi, and even the odd travesty like Schezwan, that consistency is what keeps the Bengaluru dose on top.

name: The Day the Chariot Moved
description:
There is an India hiding in plain sight, asking us to pull the chariot. 
Mindtree co-founder Subroto Bagchi returns to BIC, where he spoke in 2006 at one of the earliest programmes, to chart how his idea of the entrepreneur has changed across twenty years. What does “entrepreneur” mean once you meet the people who truly keep the world moving? 
After four decades in the corporate sector, he answered Chief Minister Naveen Patnaik’s call to work with the Government of Odisha, spending eight years there largely on skill development. In this talk, he will explore a new version of the economy, one built at the grassroots rather than in boardrooms. He will introduce the nano unicorns: ordinary people in small towns, given training and a small grant to build what they see as necessary. He will make the case that skill development is not merely a route to employability but an instrument of human transformation. 
This talk is part of a series marking twenty years of BIC, in which speakers and artists from the institution’s early years return to revisit the topics they first addressed. Each session traces what has changed, what has endured, and what to make of the same topics two decades on.

name: Miracle in Antarctica
description:
70 min | English with English subtitles | 2026 | India 
In December 1983, geophysicist and seismologist Dr. Harsh Kumar Gupta is sent to Antarctica to lead an impossible mission: build Dakshin Gangotri, India’s first scientific base station, before the end of the Antarctic summer. Given a fleeting timeframe of barely sixty days, success would set a world record. Alas, time is not his only adversary. After a blizzard and a helicopter crash, can determination outpace the pack ice? 
The screening of the film will be followed by a discussion with the protagonist and filmmakers. A Q&A with the audience will follow.

name: Marriage Cops
description:
80 min | Hindi with English subtitles | 2025 | India 
In a Dehradun police station, unhappy couples bring their marital troubles to an all-woman team of officers. Marriage Cops is an intimate observational documentary that follows three couples, from everyday domestic disputes to harrowing cases of violence and neglect, and the officers who mediate between them. What is the state doing in our bedrooms? 
The film finds no clear villains and no pure victims. Those seeking help can exercise agency despite their dire circumstances, using the state’s power to their own advantage. The police, for all their authority, can feel powerless before an institution in which entire families and communities have a stake. Moments of heartbreak sit alongside warmth and humour, as the officers shift between enforcers and counsellors. The result is a nuanced portrait of a place where traditional marriage values meet emerging ideas of women’s rights.

name: South India's Forgotten Decade of War
description:
The Nawab of Arcot was a highly coveted title in the mid-eigthteenth century Deccan, resulting in a struggle known as the Carnatic Wars. This discussion will explore how it laid the foundations of the British empire and altered the political course of the Indian subcontinent. 
The Carnatic Wars ran for decades, between local factions backed by the French and English trading companies. The military lessons learned during the conflicts at Arcot, Cuddalore, Pondicherry and Trichy were then applied by the English in their campaigns across the Indian subcontinent. This eponymous book, published by HarperCollins, offers a unique take on reading history, sans judgement, with an open mind and compassion for the human beings behind the famous names. The discussion with be followed by a Q&A with the audience.

name: The Desert, the Mystic, the Musician
description:
Some of the desert’s oldest songs live in the voices of a single community. This interactive session is an introduction to the musical heritage of the Mirs from Pugal, Rajasthan. It begins with an algozha piece showcasing the region’s iconic double flute. The evening then opens into a storytelling piece with pictures from the Thar Desert, moving on to a performance with three generations of Mirasi musicians. 
Drawing on the songs of the desert mystics across languages and folk practices, their repertoire spans the Bhakti and Sufi traditions. From Saraiki songs to those sung in regional dialects, this slowly fading tradition carries the sounds of the land and the stories of its people.

name: Breaking Rules Breaks Barriers
description:
Whose permission are you waiting for?  
This conversation reflects on entrepreneurship, reinvention, and the courage to challenge convention. Spanning four decades, three very different journeys, and two continents, the session explores how one woman built a technology company in the United States while navigating ambition, family, and personal change. 
The session is also, in part, a homecoming: a story that began with leaving India more than fifty years ago, now returning to be told in Bangalore, the heart of the country’s technology world. It makes the case for being a little edgy, for refusing to wait for anyone’s permission to break from convention.

name: Self and Society
description:
This discussion examines the tension between personal autonomy and collective life, as explored across two novels, The Convert and Bhiku and His Bowl. In this moderated session, the two authors come together to reflect on what they see as a quiet loss of spirituality within modern communes, set against the growing dominance of organised religion, followed by questions from the audience. 
Both novels draw their ethical frameworks from native religious histories, treated not as systems of divine order but as moral architectures for imagining harmonious, communal life. Their relevance lies in their optimistic vision of secular eco-villages, spaces that continually negotiate individual expression against collective responsibility. They share the philosophical question: how much of the self must be yielded to a community in exchange for its survival, equity, and well-being, and how much spiritual search can remain a private, individual pursuit even within a shared life? What does it cost a self to belong to something larger than itself?

name: Swarantar – A Mosaic of Melodies
description:
This concert explores twin ragas that differ by only a single swara, yet inhabit entirely different emotional worlds despite their near-identical scales. Presented side by side, the ragas reveal how one altered note reshapes melodic movement, how characteristic phrases diverge, and how the smallest shift in pitch can change a raga’s entire temperament. 
Ragas, the concert suggests, are not merely scales but living personalities. The comparative listening invites the audience into the mindset of composer and performer alike, showcasing the subtle moments where two melodic lines converge before parting to chart their own paths: a quiet reminder of the poetry hidden in what might otherwise pass unnoticed.
